title: THE WOMEN AT GOD’S DOOR: THE SHOCKING CONNECTION BETWEEN A SACRED MIRROR, A CORRUPT PRIESTHOOD, AND THE JESUS WHO SEES THE FORGOTTEN
paragraphs: THE WOMEN AT GOD’S DOOR: THE SHOCKING CONNECTION BETWEEN A SACRED MIRROR, A CORRUPT PRIESTHOOD, AND THE JESUS WHO SEES THE FORGOTTEN

Why does the Bible mention women serving at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting in Exodus 38:8 and 1 Samuel 2:22? Behind these easily overlooked verses lies a story of worship, betrayal, sacred service, and the Savior who refuses to let human corruption have the final word.
There are some Bible verses we read without stopping.
A name. A measurement. A strange detail about an ancient building.
We turn the page, assuming there is nothing there for us.
But sometimes, buried in a sentence we almost skipped, is a truth that will make us put the Bible down for a moment and examine our own hearts.
And this is one of those moments.
Because the Bible tells us something unusual about women standing at the entrance of God's sacred dwelling.
In one passage, their mirrors become part of a holy vessel.
In another, women associated with that same sacred entrance appear in a devastating account of priestly corruption.
Two passages.
One sacred location.
Two very different pictures of what happens when human beings approach the presence of God.

And somewhere between those pictures is a question that should disturb every person who has ever trusted a spiritual leader, served in a church, been wounded by religious hypocrisy, or wondered whether God still sees the people everyone else overlooks.
What happens when the place where people come to meet God becomes the place where they are mistreated?
And perhaps even more personally...
What does Jesus do with the people who have been wounded near the very place they came looking for Him?
To understand the answer, we have to return to the wilderness.
Before the corruption.
Before the scandal.
Before the priesthood became a warning.
We have to meet the women whose mirrors became part of Israel's worship.
Exodus 38:8 records:
"He made the laver of brass, and the foot of it of brass, of the lookingglasses of the women assembling, which assembled at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation." (KJV)
It sounds like a small construction detail.
But slow down.

Moses is describing the making of the bronze basin, a vessel placed between the altar and the entrance to the sanctuary, where the priests would wash their hands and feet before ministering (Exodus 30:17–21; 40:30–32).
And where did the bronze come from?
The mirrors belonging to women who assembled at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.
In the ancient world, mirrors were not the glass objects we use today. They were made from polished metal, often bronze, which could reflect a person's appearance.
These women possessed objects associated with looking at themselves.
And those objects became material for a basin associated with priestly cleansing.
That is what the text actually tells us.
But the Hebrew takes us somewhere even more interesting.
The phrase describing these women includes the words:
הַצֹּבְאֹת אֲשֶׁר צָבְאוּ
Hatsov'ot asher tsav'u.
The wording comes from the Hebrew root צבא (tsava'), which can carry the sense of assembling, being organized for service, or performing an assigned duty.
The same root is used in contexts involving organized groups and service, including certain Levitical responsibilities (Numbers 4:23).
This is why Bible translations differ in how they describe these women.
Some emphasize their assembling or gathering.
Others describe them as women who served or ministered at the entrance.
The Hebrew wording suggests an organized activity associated with the sanctuary, but the passage does not give us a complete description of their responsibilities.
We are not told that these women were priestesses.
We are not told that they performed sacrifices.
We are not told exactly what their daily duties involved.
And we must not invent details simply because a mysterious verse captures our imagination.
But one thing is unmistakable.
These women were not invisible to God.
Their presence was remembered.
Their contribution was recorded.
And the materials they provided became part of the sacred furnishings used in Israel's worship.
Think about that.
The book of Exodus contains astonishing details about the tabernacle.
Gold.
Silver.
Bronze.
Curtains.
Precious stones.
Priestly garments.
Exact measurements.
Specific instructions.
And right there, among the sacred construction records, Scripture pauses to acknowledge women whose mirrors were used to make the basin.
God did not need to mention that detail for us to understand the dimensions of the basin.
Yet the detail is there.
And perhaps that should challenge the way we measure significance.
Because human beings tend to remember the people standing in front.
The speakers.
The leaders.
The people whose names appear on buildings.
But God also sees the people whose names never appear on the program.
The person who cleans after everyone leaves.
The widow who gives quietly.
The exhausted mother who prays when nobody is watching.
The believer who serves without applause.
The woman who has spent years wondering whether her contribution mattered.
The man who thinks his small act of obedience will never make a difference.
The women in Exodus 38:8 are unnamed.
Yet their contribution is preserved in Scripture.
And there is something deeply comforting about serving a God who does not need the world to recognize you before He sees you.
But we must be careful with one popular interpretation.
You may have heard someone preach that these women surrendered their mirrors because they were giving up vanity, pride, or an obsession with outward beauty.
It is a memorable sermon illustration.
But Exodus does not explicitly say that.
The passage does not accuse the women of vanity.
It does not describe their mirrors as sinful.
It does not say that possessing a mirror was spiritually wrong.
What it does say is that the mirrors became material for the bronze basin.
We can draw a meaningful spiritual reflection from that transformation, but we must distinguish reflection from what Scripture directly teaches.
A mirror shows us our outward appearance.
The basin was used for ceremonial washing.
That contrast can remind us that God cares about something deeper than what other people see.
But the deeper biblical teaching comes from passages such as 1 Samuel 16:7, where God declares that human beings look at outward appearance while the LORD looks at the heart.
And from James 1:23–25, where God's Word is compared to a mirror that exposes what a person must not merely observe but respond to.
The problem is not that we have mirrors.
The problem is that we can spend our lives examining our faces while refusing to examine our hearts.
We can look presentable and remain spiritually exhausted.
We can wear the right clothes, speak the right religious language, and know exactly when to raise our hands during worship...
While hiding bitterness.
Unconfessed sin.
Jealousy.
Secret compromise.
Or a wound so deep that we have learned to smile over it.
And this is where the bronze basin becomes a powerful reminder.
The priests were commanded to wash before approaching their sacred duties.
Their position did not exempt them from God's requirements.
Their religious clothing did not make cleansing unnecessary.
Their public ministry did not remove their responsibility to approach God reverently.
And that matters because the next passage reveals what happens when religious position becomes an excuse for moral corruption.
Years later, the scene shifts to Shiloh.
The tabernacle is associated with Israel's worship there.
Eli is the priest.
His sons, Hophni and Phinehas, hold priestly positions.
And something is terribly wrong.
First Samuel 2 describes men who abused their sacred responsibilities.
They treated the LORD's offerings with contempt.
They took portions of sacrifices unlawfully.
They used their authority to satisfy their appetites rather than honor God.
Then we reach verse 22.
"Now Eli was very old, and heard all that his sons did unto all Israel; and how they lay with the women that assembled at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation." (1 Samuel 2:22, KJV)
Read that carefully.
The women are again described in connection with the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.
The Hebrew uses the same verbal root found in Exodus 38:8, creating a striking linguistic connection between the two passages.
But there is an important distinction.
The Bible does not say these were the same individual women.
The events are separated by generations.
The repeated wording points to women associated with the sanctuary entrance, not to a single group of women living across both periods.
And the text does not give us enough information to establish every detail of their role.
What it does give us is a devastating report concerning the conduct of Eli's sons.
The Hebrew expression in 1 Samuel 2:22 is:
יִשְׁכְּבוּן אֶת־הַנָּשִׁים
Yishkevun et-hannashim.
It refers to lying with the women and, in this context, describes sexual relations.
The surrounding narrative presents the conduct of Eli's sons as part of their serious wickedness.
But we must not claim more than the text reveals.
Scripture does not explicitly explain whether these sexual encounters involved coercion, threats, manipulation, or some other circumstance.
Given the men's priestly authority and the narrative's condemnation of their conduct, the possibility of exploitation is a serious concern. Yet the precise circumstances are not specified.
The women should not automatically be blamed for what the text presents as the corruption of the priests.
Nor should we turn this verse into a sensational story about supposed temple prostitution.
There is no sufficient basis in these passages to conclude that the women were cult prostitutes or that their presence at the sanctuary entrance was inherently immoral.
The biblical emphasis falls on the wickedness of Hophni and Phinehas.
And the tragedy is severe enough without adding details God did not reveal.
These were men entrusted with sacred responsibilities.
They were supposed to help preserve reverence for the LORD.
Instead, their conduct dishonored Him.
And there is something particularly disturbing about sin committed by people who occupy positions of spiritual trust.
Because when someone who claims to represent God acts wickedly, the damage can reach far beyond the immediate wrongdoing.
People can begin to associate the character of God with the character of the person who misrepresented Him.
A believer can lose confidence in spiritual leadership.
A young person can become disillusioned with the church.
A wounded person can begin to wonder whether the God they were taught to trust is anything like the people who claimed to serve Him.
And if you have ever experienced that kind of betrayal, this part of Scripture may feel painfully personal.
Maybe someone used Bible verses to silence your questions.
Maybe a person who spoke publicly about holiness lived privately in hypocrisy.
Maybe you trusted a spiritual authority who later violated that trust.
Maybe you were told to protect a ministry's reputation instead of speaking truthfully about wrongdoing.
Or maybe you simply watched people use God's name to excuse behavior that contradicted His Word.
There is something you need to see in this passage.
God did not call the wickedness of Eli's sons holy simply because they were priests.
Their position did not change the moral nature of their actions.
Their religious responsibilities did not shield them from accountability.
And their connection to the sanctuary did not make their behavior acceptable.
First Samuel 2:12 describes Eli's sons as wicked men who did not know the LORD.
Imagine that.
Men who worked around sacred things.
Men who handled religious responsibilities.
Men who belonged to a priestly family.
Yet Scripture says they did not know the LORD.
That should make every Christian examine something uncomfortable.
It is possible to become familiar with religious activity without truly walking with God.
You can know the language of worship without possessing a worshipful heart.
You can be recognized in a congregation and still resist repentance.
You can hold a title and remain spiritually rebellious.
You can teach people about holiness while secretly protecting the very sins you condemn.
And no amount of public ministry can substitute for genuine faith, obedience, and repentance.
Jesus would later issue a sobering warning in Matthew 7:21–23 about people who appealed to impressive religious works while lacking a true relationship with Him.
That warning is not an invitation to live in constant terror that every imperfect believer is secretly rejected.
It is a call to stop confusing religious performance with genuine surrender to Christ.
Because the Gospel does not merely invite us to appear righteous.
It calls us to come honestly before the only One who can save us.
And here is another detail we cannot afford to miss.
Eli knew that his sons were behaving wickedly.
He confronted them verbally.
But the biblical account shows that he failed to restrain them as he should have.
In 1 Samuel 3:13, God declares judgment against Eli's house because of the evil involving his sons and Eli's failure to restrain them.
This is not a small warning.
It means spiritual responsibility includes more than privately disapproving of wrongdoing.
It requires taking evil seriously.
Especially when people under someone's authority are being harmed or placed at risk.
A ministry does not become faithful by hiding scandal.
A church does not glorify Jesus by protecting unrepentant wrongdoing.
A leader does not honor God by preserving an image of holiness while refusing necessary accountability.
The name of Christ is not protected by concealing evil committed in His name.
It is honored when His truth is obeyed.
And that truth includes justice, repentance, care for the vulnerable, and the refusal to treat people as expendable.
If wrongdoing is happening in a spiritual community, seeking safety, reporting abuse to appropriate authorities, and pursuing responsible accountability are not acts of rebellion against God.
They can be necessary acts of truth and protection.
Forgiveness does not require silence.
Grace does not eliminate consequences.
And repentance is not a substitute for protecting people from further harm.
Now return, for a moment, to those two scenes.
In Exodus, women associated with the entrance of the Tent of Meeting contribute mirrors that become part of a basin for priestly washing.
In Samuel, women associated with the sanctuary entrance appear in a report exposing the wicked conduct of priests.
The biblical writers do not explicitly present these two accounts as a deliberate symbolic contrast.
We should not pretend that they do.
But reading them together confronts us with a meaningful theological question.
What happens when those entrusted with sacred service refuse the moral seriousness their calling demands?
The basin was a reminder that priests were not above God's requirements.
Hophni and Phinehas demonstrate the danger of behaving as though sacred office places someone beyond correction.
And that contrast points us toward a much greater need.
Because Israel did not merely need better religious appearances.
It needed faithful mediation between a holy God and sinful humanity.
And so do we.
This is where the story becomes more than a lesson about ancient women, bronze mirrors, or corrupt priests.
This is where it leads us to Jesus Christ.
The New Testament presents Jesus as the great High Priest who is fundamentally different from the sinful priests of old.
Hebrews 4:15 says:
"For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin." (KJV)
Do you see the difference?
Hophni and Phinehas used sacred responsibility while living wickedly.
Jesus exercised His ministry in perfect obedience to the Father.
Corrupt religious leaders can use authority for selfish gain.
Jesus gave Himself for the salvation of sinners.
Human priests needed cleansing.
Jesus, the sinless Son of God, became the source of the cleansing we could never accomplish through our own righteousness.
Hebrews 7:26 describes Him as holy, harmless, undefiled, and separate from sinners.
Hebrews 9 explains that Christ entered the greater heavenly sanctuary through His own blood, securing eternal redemption.
And Hebrews 10:22 speaks of drawing near to God with hearts cleansed and bodies washed with pure water.
The bronze basin did not save Israel.
It belonged to the system of worship God established under the old covenant.
Its washing was part of priestly ceremonial preparation.
But those cleansing requirements help us appreciate the holiness of God and the greater purification accomplished through Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is not that we must polish ourselves until God finally finds us acceptable.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ, who was without sin, died for sinners and rose again, and that forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered through Him.
We do not earn salvation by becoming impressive.
We receive God's grace through faith in Christ.
And the grace that saves us also calls us away from sin and into a transformed life.
That is why the message of the Gospel is so much greater than religious self-improvement.
It is redemption.
It is forgiveness.
It is reconciliation.
It is a new beginning grounded in the finished work of Jesus.
And perhaps the most beautiful part is how Jesus treated women in a world where they could so easily be dismissed.
Consider the woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years.
In Mark 5:25–34, she approached Jesus believing that touching His clothing would bring healing.
She had suffered for years.
She had spent her resources seeking help.
And her condition had left her desperate.
When she touched His garment, she was healed.
But Jesus did not simply allow her to disappear into the crowd.
He stopped.
He called attention to what had happened.
He listened to her truth.
And He addressed her with tenderness.
"Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague." (Mark 5:34, KJV)
Daughter.
Not an inconvenience.
Not a distraction.
Not an anonymous problem.
Daughter.
Now think of the Samaritan woman in John 4.
Jesus met her at a well and spoke openly about her life.
He did not pretend her past was irrelevant.
But neither did He reduce her entire identity to her history.
He revealed Himself as the Messiah, and her encounter with Him became part of the testimony that brought others to hear His words.
And consider the woman caught in adultery in John 7:53–8:11, a passage with a significant textual-history question because the earliest surviving manuscripts of John do not contain it.
In the traditional account, Jesus refuses to join the crowd's condemnation while also calling the woman to leave her sin.
The broader New Testament teaching is clear regardless of that passage's textual status.
Jesus does not make peace with sin.
But neither does He treat broken people as disposable.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He welcomes those who come to Him.
He restores people through grace and truth.
And this is the heart of our theme:
Not because scandal is insignificant.
Not because evil should be forgotten.
Not because repentance is optional.
And certainly not because every wound disappears the moment someone says a prayer.
Jesus rewrites lives because His death and resurrection accomplish what human religion cannot.
He forgives the repentant sinner.
He brings the spiritually dead to life.
He gives hope to the wounded.
He calls the proud to humility.
He confronts hypocrisy.
He establishes a new identity for those who belong to Him.
And He promises a final restoration in which evil will not have the last word.
But notice something.
Jesus does not rewrite the past by pretending it never happened.
The Bible itself preserves the scandal of Eli's sons.
Their wickedness is not erased from Scripture.
It is exposed.
Why?
Because grace is not the same thing as denial.
The Gospel is powerful precisely because it tells the truth about sin and then reveals a Savior powerful enough to redeem sinners.
There is no need to minimize darkness to magnify the light.
And that brings us to a question that is no longer about ancient Israel.
It is about you.
What are you carrying into the presence of God today?
Is it guilt?
Is it shame?
Is it anger toward someone who misused spiritual authority?
Is it a secret you have been too afraid to confess?
Is it disappointment because people who claimed to represent Jesus failed to reflect His character?
Or is it the quiet exhaustion of serving God while wondering whether anybody notices?
Perhaps you recognize yourself in the unnamed women of Exodus.
You have given.
You have served.
You have sacrificed.
You have shown up when nobody applauded.
And you have wondered whether your obedience matters.
Remember that Scripture preserved the contribution of women whose individual names were not recorded.
The God who sees in secret is not indifferent to faithful service.
Or perhaps you recognize the pain that can surround 1 Samuel 2.
You came near a religious community hoping to encounter truth, only to discover hypocrisy.
You trusted someone who should have acted responsibly.
You heard people speak about holiness while refusing to confront wrongdoing.
If that is part of your story, do not confuse the failures of sinful people with the character of the sinless Christ.
Jesus is not another Hophni.
Jesus is not another Phinehas.
He is the faithful High Priest.
He does not need to exploit people to preserve His position.
He does not use spiritual authority to satisfy selfish appetites.
He does not excuse evil because the offender holds an impressive title.
He is righteous.
He is holy.
He is merciful.
And He is worthy of your trust.
That does not mean you must immediately trust every religious institution or leader again.
Trust can require time, demonstrated integrity, and accountability.
But the failures of human beings do not cancel the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this is not primarily wounded by another person's sin.
Perhaps you are confronted by your own.
You have become very good at looking spiritually presentable.
You know how to answer, "How are you?"
You know how to smile.
You know how to post Scripture.
You know how to appear strong.
But behind closed doors, you know there are things that need to change.
And you are tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of hiding.
Tired of promising yourself that tomorrow will be different.
Then hear the invitation of the Gospel.
You do not have to protect your image before Jesus.
He already knows the truth.
And the One who knows the truth is the very One who calls sinners to come to Him.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
Not because confession purchases forgiveness.
Not because we have finally become worthy.
But because God's forgiveness rests on the righteous and sufficient work of Jesus Christ.
So stop confusing concealment with safety.
Stop calling spiritual exhaustion normal.
Stop defending the sin that is destroying your peace.
And stop believing that your worst chapter must become your final identity.
Turn to Christ.
Tell Him the truth.
Repent of what needs repentance.
Seek help where help is needed.
Make restitution where it is possible and appropriate.
And receive the grace that cannot be purchased with good behavior.
You may not be able to undo yesterday.
But in Christ, yesterday does not have to rule tomorrow.
That is not permission to escape responsibility.
It is hope for genuine transformation.
And if you have witnessed God's mercy in a season when you thought your life was beyond repair, share a little of your testimony.
You do not have to reveal private details or painful experiences publicly.
God hears prayers that never appear in a comment section.
But your willingness to speak honestly, even in a few simple words, may encourage another person who thought they were struggling alone.
And please do not let this message end with you.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
Not because an algorithm measures your faithfulness.
But because someone in your circle may desperately need to understand that religious hypocrisy is not the same as the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Someone may be ready to abandon faith because of what a human leader did.
Someone may be carrying shame they have never told anyone about.
Someone may be faithfully serving in obscurity and wondering whether God sees.
Or send this privately to a family member who needs to remember that Christ remains faithful even when people fail.
Come back to the passages.
Read Exodus 38.
Read 1 Samuel 2 and 3.
Read Hebrews 4, 7, 9, and 10.
Do not build your understanding of Scripture on a single emotional message, including this one.
Open the Bible for yourself.
Examine the context.
Ask questions.
Grow in discernment.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, Christians who have grown spiritually complacent, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along.
There is room for honest questions.
There is room to learn.
There is room to be challenged by Scripture.
And there is room to discover that the Gospel is far more beautiful than the religious performances people sometimes mistake for Christianity.
These resources are intended to help believers become more grounded in Scripture, more discerning about biblical truth, and more mature in their walk with Jesus Christ.
And there is another invitation I want to extend with sincerity.
Not because you must pay to receive God's grace.
And not because anyone should feel guilty if they cannot afford to give.
The Gospel is not for sale.
But sharing biblical teaching, developing discipleship resources, preparing books, and expanding outreach can involve real costs.
It is a practical way to participate in the mission of making Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources available to more people.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, not under compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
But it can be a meaningful voluntary offering toward Christian teaching and outreach.
They are not spiritual rewards.
The greatest gift is still the Gospel itself.
And that gift cannot be bought.
That Jesus Christ would be known.
That His Word would be understood faithfully.
That people would turn from sin and find forgiveness in Him.
That wounded hearts would encounter truth and compassion.
And that believers would grow beyond religious appearances into genuine discipleship.
Because when everything else is stripped away, this is what matters.
Not how impressive our ministry looks.
Not how many people applaud.
Not how many religious titles we accumulate.
Not how polished our public image becomes.
But whether we truly know Jesus Christ and are being transformed by His grace.
Remember the women at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.
Remember the mirrors that became part of a vessel used for priestly washing.
Remember the wickedness of priests who dishonored their sacred calling.
And remember the faithful High Priest who came to accomplish what no sinful priest could ever accomplish.
The women of Exodus remind us that seemingly overlooked service can matter.
The scandal in Samuel reminds us that religious authority must never be confused with righteousness.
And Jesus reminds us that our ultimate hope is not in the perfection of human leaders but in the perfection of our Savior.
One day, every earthly title will lose its importance.
Every carefully managed reputation will be exposed to the truth.
Every hidden thing will stand before the righteous judgment of God.
And the only righteousness sufficient to save sinners will be the righteousness found in Jesus Christ.
So do not spend your entire life polishing the mirror while neglecting the condition of your soul.
Do not spend your entire life admiring religious appearances while refusing the cleansing only Christ can give.
And do not allow the failures of those who misrepresented Him to make you forget the One who never failed.
The story began with women whose mirrors were used in a sacred basin.
It passed through a painful account of men who corrupted their sacred responsibilities.
But it brings us, finally, to a Savior who is holy, compassionate, and faithful forever.
And perhaps that is the truth someone reading this has been waiting to hear.
You are not saved by looking clean.
You are saved by Jesus Christ.
You are not healed by pretending the wound never happened.
You can bring the truth of your suffering before the Savior who sees.
You are not made righteous by standing near holy things.
You need the grace of the Holy One Himself.
And your past, however painful, does not have to be the final chapter of your life.
The hands that were pierced for your redemption are still more trustworthy than every hand that ever failed you.
